children: Rising temperatures and groundwater depletion are exposing vulnerabilities in India’s agricultural system, prompting calls for water-efficient farming technologies, watershed restoration and stronger community participation

Rising temperatures and mounting pressure on freshwater resources are exposing the limitations of India’s traditional agricultural practices, strengthening the case for climate-resilient farming and community-led water management. With agriculture accounting for more than 90 per cent of India’s freshwater withdrawals and nearly a quarter of groundwater assessment units facing varying degrees of stress, experts are calling for greater investment in water-efficient technologies and long-term resource management.

India’s changing climate is adding to the challenge. According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), 10 of the country’s 15 warmest years were recorded between 2011 and 2025. The winter season of January-February 2025 was also the warmest on record since 1901.

The pressure on water resources is equally significant. The 2025 Dynamic Ground Water Resources Assessment, conducted by the Central Ground Water Board and state governments, found that 1,689 of India’s 6,762 groundwater assessment units were classified as semi-critical, critical or over-exploited.

Arvind Narayanan, Co-Founder of Growize Farms, said the country’s agricultural adaptation challenge was increasingly about implementing solutions rather than building awareness about climate change. “India’s water and agricultural adaptation gap isn’t about awareness; it’s about action. Every farmer in the country is well aware that the seasons are getting hotter. Our farming system was designed for a climate that no longer exists,” he said.

One approach gaining attention is controlled-environment agriculture, particularly aeroponic farming, which allows crops to grow without conventional soil cultivation. Narayanan highlighted the potential of aeroponics to reduce water consumption in vegetable and leafy green production while improving productivity per unit of land.

According to Growize Farms, its aeroponic farming model uses up to 95 per cent less water than conventional cultivation and can deliver up to three times the yield. The company also says its controlled growing systems enable year-round production and reduce dependence on pesticides.
Narayanan said such systems could complement conventional farming rather than replace staple crops such as wheat and paddy.

“Wheat and paddy won’t go into a controlled environment. Vegetables and leafy greens can and should,” he said. He added that expanding precision farming facilities closer to consumption centres could help reduce pressure on agricultural land and freshwater resources.

“Growing more of this on precision farms with quick access to markets frees up water and land for staples. We have the technology. We just need the finance and policy to treat controlled-environment farming as climate infrastructure,” Narayanan said. However, wider adoption would depend on financing, infrastructure and policy support to make such technologies commercially viable and accessible at scale.

Alongside technological interventions, ecological restoration and community participation are becoming important components of climate adaptation, particularly in water-stressed rural regions. Tata Communications said its environmental initiatives integrate climate action, biodiversity, water conservation and energy management into community development programmes.
A Tata Communications spokesperson said local participation was essential to ensuring the sustainability of environmental restoration projects.

“Keeping the community at the centre of development is key. Environmental CSR frameworks must be built to ensure that local Panchayats, women’s self-help groups, and youth become active custodians,” the spokesperson said.

The company cited Project Nanneer, an initiative focused on restoring Nagan Thangal Lake in Tamil Nadu, as an example of its water conservation efforts. The project has enhanced the lake’s water-holding capacity and supported groundwater recharge. According to Tata Communications, the restoration has improved groundwater recharge, provided drinking water for livestock and supported occasional fishing and community recreation. The initiative has improved the quality of life of nearly 12,000 people, around 60 per cent of whom belong to marginalised communities.

The company is also implementing its Vitalize Rural programme in water-stressed areas such as Dharashiv in Maharashtra, working with specialist organisations on integrated watershed management. The programme focuses on soil moisture retention, aquifer replenishment and climate-resilient agriculture to strengthen rural livelihoods against delayed monsoons and recurring droughts. The spokesperson said establishing community learning centres alongside ecological restoration could help make water security a locally sustained practice rather than a corporate social responsibility exercise.

As climate pressures intensify, India’s adaptation strategy will increasingly depend on combining technological interventions with better management of natural resources. Expanding water-efficient agricultural systems, improving access to finance and strengthening community ownership of local water bodies will remain important to protecting rural livelihoods and improving long-term water security.
